prize_parts.citation: for visionary, densely patterned prose that fuses memory, the body and dream into a metaphysical architecture of the novel

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged: Cărtărescu, one writer, one prize part, with a citation that rests on the prose. The criterion that decides it for me is distinctiveness of voice. The Orbitor trilogy (Blinding is its first part) and Solenoid, by public critical accounts, show a voice that is hard to place anywhere else. It treats memory, the body, dream and the city as one metaphysical project, and the density of the sentence is part of that project and not decoration. The formal achievement is the construction of very large narrative structures from that material. The imaginative and intellectual depth comes from the sustained construction, not from range of theme. The chair asked what would show development and not repetition. I can offer only public knowledge: the Orbitor trilogy is built as a large, mythically and anatomically organised structure, while Solenoid is widely described as a different construction, with a more first-person, diary-like and everyday frame that is broken open by visionary material. If that description holds, Solenoid is a late reorganisation of the earlier concerns and not a copy. I have not verified this by close reading. I keep the poetry out of the citation because I cannot support a poetry-and-prose claim with what I know, and the prose carries the case. This is a judgment on voice, form and depth. It does not depend on how many colleagues share it.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is unchanged. The achievement lies largely in Romanian sentence rhythm and density, which I can judge only through translation and public critical knowledge. The encyclopedic length of the late books may be sustained invention or excess, and I cannot settle that from the supplied evidence. This exchange has also weakened one of my round-1 objections to Carson. Olsson and Palm now say they would draft the citation around her own lyric, verse narrative and essay, with antiquity as the field of dialogue and translation, scholarship and book design as context only. That addresses much of my worry about citation scope. The remaining doubts are whether depth holds beyond Autobiography of Red and Nox, and whether the later output is as strong as the central books. If the committee found that the late Cărtărescu volumes mostly rework Orbitor's motifs without a new structural principle, my preference would weaken, and Carson would be the first alternative I would weigh seriously against him.

responses.point: Olsson prefers Carson and has now said he would draft the citation around the renewal of lyric, essay and verse narrative, with antiquity as the field of dialogue. He argues that a few works of lasting formal importance within a consistent method can meet an oeuvre standard, and that volume is not required. He also names the opposite worry for Carson, that concision and variety might hide a lack of depth.
responses.response: Your narrowed citation answers my scope objection. I withdraw the claim that her output is too hard to delimit, and I now treat that as a drafting problem and not a literary one. I also accept your point that volume is not the standard. I make the same argument for Michon, so I cannot use length against Carson and then reject it as a criterion for him. What remains for me is evidence. Whether the later books develop the concerns of the fragment, loss and the afterlife of ancient texts, or only vary the format, is something I cannot test from what I know, and you say you cannot test it fully either. The point where I still differ is how the two cases can be checked. Cărtărescu's claim can be tested against a few named volumes in a single form, while hers requires judging a hybrid corpus. I count that as a difference in checkability and not in merit. This is why I keep Carson as my first alternative and no longer give her lower weight.

responses.point: Palm prefers Carson. She argues that the translations and adaptations belong to the same project of treating the classical text as a fragment, that the central books work through emotional and formal movement without requiring the reader to hold the sources in mind, and that the committee should say openly that confidence in the later output is lower than in the central books. She also wants Cărtărescu's length tested against sustained quality.
responses.response: I accept your candour about the later work, and I think the committee should say the same of Cărtărescu: our confidence in the late volumes rests on public accounts, not on verified reading. Your distinction between difficulty of reference and limited significance corrects something in my round-1 reasoning. I had treated the allusive and book-object elements as a barrier to assessing the whole oeuvre, and your account suggests that the central books can be read on the page. I still disagree that translations can be folded into her own oeuvre. A citation can name the project of reworking the fragment without crediting translation, as you propose, and I would want that stated explicitly. On your test for Cărtărescu, I agree that scale cannot count as evidence. My stated condition is that the late books must show a new structural principle and not only more of the same. That is the evidence I would look for.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg prefers Cărtărescu and proposes comparing the Orbitor trilogy with Solenoid for real development. He accepts that a Nobel oeuvre can contain weaker volumes if the peaks are sustained, and he places Michon third, arguing that a small corpus gives less evidence of range.
responses.response: I agree with your comparison as the test and have used it in my case above, with the limit that I can offer only public accounts of both works. On Michon, my round-1 reply to you stands, but I would sharpen it. A slim corpus does not disqualify a writer under a whole-authorship standard, though it leaves the claim to sustained quality resting on fewer works. Together with the probable loss in translating compressed French, that is why I have moved Michon to second alternative and Carson to first. This is a change in how I order the alternatives, not a statement about the quality of his prose, which I still find exceptional.

responses.point: Carlberg prefers Cărtărescu and would treat the case as one about voice, language and imaginative depth. She names Carson as the more convincing alternative if the late volumes proved inflated, and she asks for a more specific account of Adonis's later poetry. She says she cannot confirm the poetry-and-prose continuum claim in her own citation.
responses.response: Your conditional about Carson matches mine, and I take it as a shared fallback and not as a prediction. Because you say you cannot confirm the continuum between the poetry and the prose, I would ask you and Sem-Sandberg to drop 'and poetry' from the citation. A public statement that the committee cannot support would be a weaker citation. On Adonis, I cannot offer the specific account of the later poetry that you ask for. I rated him third in my opening on his reshaping of Arabic poetic language over a very long career, but I judge that mostly through translation. Without such an account I have also moved him out of my two named alternatives, rather than rely on a ranking I cannot defend in detail.

uncertainties: My judgment of Cărtărescu depends on translations and public critical knowledge, not on a complete reading, and the Romanian register may be only partly conveyed.
I cannot confirm from public knowledge alone that Solenoid reorganises the Orbitor project and does not repeat it. It is the central unresolved point for my preference.
Coverage of the poetry and early work is thin, and I cannot say how much weight, if any, they should carry in a citation.

For Carson, I cannot test whether depth holds beyond Autobiography of Red and Nox, and I cannot assess book-object and performance works on the page alone. The narrowed citation settles the scope question but not the maturity question.
For Michon and Adonis, translation loss is probably large and I know the later work of both only partially. My ordering of them is provisional.
Carlberg's committee voting status is undocumented, so any reading of the exchange that depends on her vote is a modelling assumption.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. I am a novelist and critic of historical and psychological fiction and a member of the Swedish Academy, and I list this only as context. It is not evidence of preference for any shortlisted writer, and no personal or institutional tie to any of them is documented. I have not independently verified any colleague's disclosures.
